note.note:
Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  - Wheezy sensation and shortness of breath beginning ~2 days ago after cleaning carpet and exposure to dust; patient suspects dust allergy.
- Symptom timeline and progression:
  - Symptoms began approximately 2 days ago, onset about 1 hour after cleaning.
  - Gradually worse over 2 days; worse at night.
  - Today more severe with difficulty speaking and inability at times to complete sentences.
- ENT symptoms:
  - Throat swelling/closure sensation: Not reported.
  - Voice change/hoarseness: Not reported.
  - Dysphagia/odynophagia: Not reported.
  - Drooling: Not reported.
  - Nasal/ocular symptoms: History of seasonal hay fever in summer; no acute nasal/ocular symptoms reported for this episode.
  - Stridor/noisy breathing: Not reported; described as “wheezy.”
  - Dyspnea: Yes — shortness of breath, worse with talking.
  - Distribution of swelling (lips/tongue/uvula/face): No swelling reported.
  - Ear/neck symptoms: Not reported.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments:
  - Childhood asthma; currently uses an asthma inhaler intermittently (patient believes she has one from a couple of months ago).
  - Occasional exercise-induced symptoms.
  - Prior use of oral steroids for asthma in the past (dose/route/frequency not documented).
  - Occasional seasonal hay fever.
  - No prior ED visits or epinephrine/injector use mentioned.
- Allergies and current medications:
  - Allergies: “Not that I know of.”
  - Current medications: asthma inhaler (name/dose/route/frequency not documented); no antihistamines at home.
- Social/contextual:
  - Patient is at home in a private/quiet space.
  - Patient is minutes’ drive from a GP surgery.

Objective:
- Observable swelling and distribution: No swelling noted or reported.
- Airway/breathing descriptors:
  - Wheeze reported by patient.
  - Shortness of breath; difficulty speaking/ completing sentences when symptomatic.
  - No stridor or noisy breathing recorded.
- Mental status and associated features:
  - Alert; no dizziness or syncope reported.
- Vitals and examination findings: Not recorded.
- Presence of another person with the patient: Not stated.

Assessment:
- Clinical impression:
  - Acute wheezy respiratory episode likely secondary to either an asthma exacerbation or allergic reaction triggered by dust exposure.
- Key justifications from transcript:
  - Recent dust exposure while cleaning (temporal association).
  - Past history of childhood asthma and seasonal hay fever.
  - Progressive wheeze over 2 days, worse at night, with current shortness of breath and speech difficulty.
- Conflict noted:
  - None apparent in clinical statements. (Video signal loss occurred during the consult; no conflicting clinical content identified.)

Plan:
- Immediate actions taken/advised:
  - Arrange in-person assessment at clinic/GP for further tests including pulse oximetry and evaluation to distinguish asthma vs allergic reaction.
  - If patient has an oral antihistamine at home, advised to take one; patient reports none available.
  - Patient advised that antihistamines are available over the counter and could be obtained en route to GP (cost estimate provided by clinician in consult).
  - Clinician will send a letter to the patient’s GP via the app to notify them of the episode and request in-person assessment.
  - Possible prescription/administration of oral steroids may be needed after in-person assessment and tests (dose/route/frequency to be determined by GP).
- Specific instructions provided to patient:
  - Attend GP/clinic in person for testing (pulse oximetry) and further management; in-person visit expected to take ~10 minutes.
  - Obtain an antihistamine OTC if needed on the way to the GP.
- Escalation criteria / red flags:
  - Not explicitly stated in transcript.
- Follow-up:
  - GP/clinic assessment in person; results will determine need for steroids or further treatment.
  - Letter to GP to be provided via app for continuity.
  - No discussion in transcript regarding allergy testing, ENT/allergy referral, auto-injector prescription, or specific inhaler use instructions.
- COVID-19 vaccine suitability: Not discussed.
- Emergency contact instructions: None provided in the transcript.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Objective vital signs (respiratory rate, heart rate, oxygen saturation), lung auscultation findings, and peak expiratory flow measurement.
  - Specific inhaler type/name and current usage details (dose/route/frequency).
  - Details of prior steroid courses (dose/route/frequency).
  - Explicit emergency/red flag instructions (when to call EMS).
  - Documentation of any prior severe reactions/anaphylaxis or availability of an auto-injector.
  - Medication dosing and routes for any recommended treatments.
- Internal conflicts from transcript:
  - None identified.
- Transcript quality comment:
  - Generally intelligible; brief video/signal interruption noted and some intermittent hesitancy in speech, but clinical content is clear.
